Reflecting then with myself that so many hands, which were diligently kept busy in producing the printing of the book, and the men by whose counsels those hands were directed, are now pressed down by the oblivion of posterity, I know not what I should say? Those men, had they remained alive, would surely have grieved, if they had learned that after death the memory of themselves, the memory of their virtues, the memory of their good deeds would fall away from the minds of men. Now, however, I do not doubt that these men feel quite otherwise. Sunday, the 31st of July. [Latin] For lack of any other material, I shall narrate in a few words the calamities of Adrastus. Adrastus, son of the king of Phrygia, etc.

o: Montag den 1. August. De Graecae linguae difficultate saepius mecum reputans has fere reperi causas. Graeci, coaevorum facile doctissimi, politissimi, fortissimi, barbarorum literas parce omnino didicerunt; cum barbaris gentibus, quas ut rudes contemserunt, parva erat illis consuetudo. Oppressorum populorum linguas victores vel deleverunt [p. 438] suamque intulerunt, vel inter plebem solam serpere passi sunt. Qua in linguarum ruditate paternam magis excoluerunt, ampliaverunt. Qua ex re maxima Graecarum literarum orta est opulentia, quae plurimas peregrino parit difficultates. Mittwoch den 3. August. Magnum cumulum addiderunt formae civitatum illimitata libertate. Summa plerumque rerum plebi subjecta, si quis valere aliquid aut efficere studuit, nihil potius esse debuit, quam auram popularem captare et sic consilia perficere. Sagaciorem non diu fugit, ad omnia adduci plebem oris eloquentia. Eo diligentius huic incubuerunt et linguam ad elegantiam et venustatem con- formarunt. Donnerstag den 4. August. Accedit multitudo, elegantia et ornatus Particularum. Numerum vero Graecorum imitari nostro tempore sane non valemus, cum pessimarum vocum usu plane sit depravatus. Sonntag den 7. August. Primo interfui hodie divino Catholicorum cultui orationique sacrae, quam a Werkmeister concionatus est. Missa, quam vocant, nondum erat finita, cum venirem, quae quidem mihi, ut sano cuivis hominum, maxime displicuit. Hymno decantato, ipsa secuta est oratio, quae mihi ita placuit, ut saepius hanc concionem adire statuerim. Spectavit tota eo, ut rudibus rigideque duram vetustatem retinentibus mitiora, aliorum Christianorum, licet a suis doctrinis differentium amantiora conformaret ingenia. Non auditum ne unum quidem verbum, ex quo conspici potuisset flebilis illa Christia- norum discordia. Montag den 8. August. Silentio non praetermittendum sane esse in hac factorum enarratione, in Collegio Rev. Dni. Prof. Clessii praestantissimas Livii historias sub DEI auspiciis nos hodie inchoasse. Libata est a summe rever. Professore Livii vita, de qua quidem pauca ad nos pervenerunt. Quae equidem didici, paucis commemorabo. Livius Patavinus sub Augusto floruit etc. Sonntag den 21. August. Interfui hodie Catholicorum iterum sacris. Majer interpretatus est Catechismum, quae quidem expositio et venerabili interpretis eruditione et maxima perspicuitate mire mihi placuit. Ante meridiem recens cooptatus arcessitusque rei divinae minister publicam habuit de virtute orationem, cui quidem me non adfuisse valde poenituit.
e: Monday, the 1st of August. [Latin] Reflecting rather often with myself on the difficulty of the Greek language, I have found, roughly, these causes. The Greeks, easily the most learned, the most polished, the bravest of their contemporaries, learned the letters of the barbarians only sparingly; with barbarian peoples, whom as rude they despised, they had little intercourse. The languages of oppressed peoples the victors either destroyed [p. 438] [Latin] and brought in their own, or allowed them to creep about only among the common people. In this rudeness of languages they cultivated and enlarged their native tongue all the more. From this arose the very great wealth of Greek letters, which causes the foreigner a great many difficulties. Wednesday, the 3rd of August. [Latin] The unlimited liberty of the form of their states added a great heap. Since supreme power was for the most part subject to the people, whoever strove to have any weight or to accomplish anything had to do nothing rather than court popular favor, and so carry through his plans. It did not long escape the more sagacious that the people could be led to anything by eloquence of speech. All the more diligently did they apply themselves to it, and shaped the language to elegance and charm. Thursday, the 4th of August. [Latin] To this is added the multitude, elegance and ornament of the particles. The rhythm of the Greeks, however, we are in our time certainly unable to imitate, since it has been utterly corrupted by the use of the worst words. Sunday, the 7th of August. [Latin] Today for the first time I attended the divine service of the Catholics and the sacred oration which Werkmeister preached. The Mass, as they call it, was not yet finished when I arrived; it displeased me exceedingly, as it would any sane man. After a hymn had been sung, the oration itself followed, which pleased me so much that I resolved to attend this preacher more often. Its whole aim was to make the minds of the uncultivated, who rigidly retain harsh antiquity, milder and more loving towards other Christians, even though these differ from their own doctrines. Not a single word was heard from which that lamentable discord of the Christians could have been discerned. Monday, the 8th of August. [Latin] It must surely not be passed over in silence in this narration of events that today, under God’s auspices, we began the most excellent histories of Livy in the class of the Reverend Professor Cless. The most reverend professor touched on the life of Livy, of which indeed little has come down to us. What I learned I shall record in a few words. Livy of Padua flourished under Augustus, etc. Sunday, the 21st of August. [Latin] Today I again attended the sacred rites of the Catholics. Majer expounded the Catechism, and this exposition pleased me wonderfully both by the venerable learning of the expositor and by its very great perspicuity. Before noon a minister of divine things, recently co-opted and called, gave a public oration on virtue, and I greatly regretted not having been present at it.

o: Montag den 22. August. Saepius et ego mecum ipse reputavi et libris etiam quae perpendantur digna reperi, quaenam sit vehementissima animi perturbatio, quae plurimas intulerit in homines, urbes, [p. 439] civitates, regna calamitates? Videamus igitur, quae effecerint honoris libido, auri, amor, superbia, invidia, desperatio, odium, ira et ultionis libido. Dienstag den 23. August. Procul dubio honoris libido publicas clades maximas attulit, sociata cum imperii cupidine. Quid Alexandrum M. Dario, a quo nunquam laesus fuit, funestissimum bellum ut inferret, impulit? Quid Timurem, Persiae regem, qui Asiam longe lateque victoribus Tartaris, victricibus armis immensa gloria peragravit? Quid tot praestantissimos Romanorum duces, quos referre immensi esset operis? Nonne haec commotio Academicis immisit funestissima certamina, quae duella vocant, quae tot florentium juvenum stamina, tot unica parentum solamina et gaudia dissecuerunt? Mittwoch den 24. August. Inter barbaras rudesque gentes virtutis non est alius impulsus praeter honorem et patriae, parentum, uxorum, liberorum amorem? Idem de majoribus nostris constat, devastasse illos immensa agrorum arvorumque spatia et inferis adjunxisse infinitum hominum numerum, ut nomen sibi per vicinitatem non solum, sed totam Germaniam acquirerent. Hactenus de honoris cupidine. Ad alia redeamus. Hier solgt im Tagebuch eine Unterbrechung bis zum December. Die Ursache erzählt Hegel selbst. Er hatte sich zu einem Examen bei bereits angegriffener Gesundheit angestrengt und bekam eine Geschwulst am Halse, welche ihm der Arzt Conspruch und der Chirurg Mohrstadt heilten. V. a. Id. Decb. Constitutum habeo, diarium hoc, et per examen nostrum Prid. Non. et ipsis Non. Septembr. habitum, et potissimum, qui me invasit, per morbum et gravem et diuturnum, longo temporis intervallo intermissum, jam resumere et pristina studia stylo exercendo renovare. Cujus igitur juvabit, temporis historiam brevi percurrere.
e: Monday, the 22nd of August. [Latin] I too have often reflected by myself, and have also found in books things worthy of being weighed, which is the most violent perturbation of the mind, the one that has brought the most calamities upon men, cities, [p. 439] states, kingdoms? Let us see, therefore, what the desire for honor, the love of gold, pride, envy, despair, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge have brought about. Tuesday, the 23rd of August. [Latin] Beyond doubt the desire for honor has brought the greatest public disasters, allied with the lust for dominion. What drove Alexander the Great to wage a most deadly war against Darius, by whom he had never been harmed? What Timur, king of Persia, who with Tartar victors, with victorious arms and immense glory ranged over Asia far and wide? What so many most distinguished leaders of the Romans, whom to enumerate would be a task of immense labor? Has not this commotion sent upon academic youth the most deadly contests, which they call duels, which have cut the threads of so many flourishing youths, so many only consolations and joys of parents? Wednesday, the 24th of August. [Latin] Among barbarous and rude peoples is there any other impulse of virtue besides honor and love of fatherland, parents, wives, children? The same is established concerning our ancestors, that they laid waste immense stretches of fields and farmlands and sent to the dead an infinite number of men, in order to acquire a name for themselves not only through their neighborhood but through all Germany. So far on the desire for honor. Let us return to other things. Here there follows in the diary an interruption until December. Hegel himself relates the cause. He had exerted himself for an examination with his health already impaired and got a swelling on the neck, which the physician Conspruch and the surgeon Mohrstadt cured. [Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of December. I have resolved to resume now this diary, interrupted for a long interval of time by the examination held by us on the day before the Nones and on the Nones of September themselves, and most of all by the illness, both grave and lasting, which seized me, and to renew my former studies by exercising my style. It will therefore be pleasing to run briefly through the history of that time.

o: Aliquot ante examen diebus jam valetudine aliquantum fessus, tamen me non cohibui, quin illud examen, dissuadentibus et edoctoribus et aliis, adirem. Feliciter illo absoluto, domus nostrae limen ulterius egressus non sum. Vehementi morbo correptus, ereptus tamen medici diligentia et medicamentis mature adhibitis. Collo sinistra parte valde intumui, omni morbi peste et sanie illuc collecta. Diu multumque hoc inflatu discruciato arte Chirurgii Mohrstadtii Medicique Conspruchii laxamentum allatum, quorum quidem prior, dissecto tumore, vulnus duarum pollicis latitudinis inflixit, ut saniei cruorisque tetra copia [p. 440] emanaret paene per triduum, quod diligentia Chirurgii frequentique deligatione inter dies circiter triginta coaluit, a secto enim vulnere a. d. VI. Non. Oct. Gymnasium rursus pridie Calend. Novb. frequentavi. IV. Id. Debr. Quae dum mecum agebantur, multa alia extra me memoria digna contigerunt. Carissimus mihi amicus ablatus est a nobis Tubingam Theologiae consecraneus, puto J. F. Duttenhoferum. Mortuus est eodem temporis spatio celeberrimus ille, decus maximum patriae nostrae Moser, qui tot, quot perlegere humana non sufficit aetas, perscripsit libros, qui tot tamque variis (casibus) jactatus vitam egit. Mortuus est dignitate insignis rebusque aliis, quas hic referre alienum est, Hochsteter. Mortuus est denique ille et genere et opibus clarus de Herzberg. III. Id. Debr. Aucta etiam est interea bibliothecula mea libris aliquot. Emi enim jam dudum: 1. Livium, ex meo aerario sumtibus erogatis, quatuor florenis; 2. Ernesti Clavim Ciceronianam, thalero; 3. Ciceronis Epistolas ad Atticum decem crucigeris; 4. Theophronem Campei, vernaculo idiomate, viginti et sex crucigeris; 5. Homei artem criticam, ex Anglica traductam in vernaculam a Meinhardo, floreno et quadraginta et quinque crucigeris; 6. Senecae opera philosophica crucigeris quindecim. Pridie Id. Debr. Quaestio hodie cum orta esset inter nos, praestare repetitio praeparationi aut haec illi, meum semper judicium fuit, optime utramvis jungi. Si vero defuerit altera alteri, equidem praeferendam esse repetitionem praeparationi. Intelligimus enim praeparati rem, ut ita dicam, dimidiam, nec vel totum haurimus sensum vel sinistrum. Edocti vero praeceptore et integrum, justum genuinumque sensum percipimus, qui repetitus menti sempiternus fere inducitur. Sed praeparati falsa verborum vi accepta, quae explanavit doctor, non diu, nisi repetatur, haeret et mox evanescit. Nobilibus hodie praesentibus Stuttgardiae peregrinis, publica musica vocum, nervorum cornuumque cantibus instituta est. Ipsis Id. Debr. Sollemnis hodie celebrata est et morum et studiorum VI classis auditorum perlustratio, quam vocant percursum, Durchgang. Hesterno die VII classis inquirebatur.
e: Some days before the examination, already somewhat wearied by ill health, I nevertheless did not restrain myself from going to that examination, though my teachers and others dissuaded me. That having happily been completed, I did not go beyond the threshold of our house again. Seized by a violent illness, I was nevertheless rescued by the diligence of the physician and by medicines promptly applied. I swelled greatly in the neck on the left side, all the poison and corruption of the disease having collected there. After long and much torment from this swelling, relief was brought by the art of the surgeon Mohrstadt and the physician Conspruch, of whom the former, having cut open the tumor, inflicted a wound two thumb-widths wide, so that a foul abundance of pus and blood [p. 440] flowed out for almost three days; which, by the diligence of the surgeon and frequent bandaging, closed up within about thirty days; for from the cutting of the wound, on the 6th day before the Nones of October, I attended the Gymnasium again on the day before the Calends of November. [Latin] The 4th day before the Ides of December. While these things were being done with me, many other things worthy of memory happened apart from me. A most dear friend of mine was taken from us to Tübingen, one dedicated to theology, I think J. F. Duttenhofer. At the same span of time died that most celebrated man, the greatest ornament of our fatherland, Moser, who wrote so many books, as many as a human lifetime does not suffice to read through, who lived a life tossed about by so many and so various (chances). Died, distinguished in dignity and in other things which it is not fitting to relate here, Hochsteter. Died finally that man, illustrious in birth and wealth, de Herzberg. [Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of December. My little library too has meanwhile been increased by some books. For I bought some time ago: 1. Livy, from my own treasury, at the expense of four florins; 2. Ernesti’s Ciceronian Key [Clavis Ciceroniana], for a thaler; 3. Cicero’s Letters to Atticus, for ten kreuzer; 4. Campe’s Theophron, in the vernacular, for twenty-six kreuzer; 5. Home’s art of criticism, translated from English into the vernacular by Meinhard, for one florin and forty-five kreuzer; 6. Seneca’s philosophical works for fifteen kreuzer. [Latin] The day before the Ides of December. A question having arisen today among us, whether repetition is better than preparation or the latter than the former, my judgment has always been that it is best for either to be joined with the other. If, however, one of the two should be lacking to the other, I for my part would hold that repetition should be preferred to preparation. For when we have prepared, we understand the matter, so to speak, only by half, and we draw out either not the whole sense or a perverse one. But when taught by the preceptor, we perceive the whole, just and genuine sense, which, repeated, is implanted in the mind almost for ever. But when we have prepared, the force of the words having been taken falsely, what the teacher has explained does not stick long unless it is repeated, and soon vanishes. Noble visitors being present today at Stuttgart, public music of voices, strings and horns was arranged. [Latin] On the Ides of December itself. Today the solemn inspection of the morals and studies of the auditors of the sixth class was held, which they call percursum, Durchgang [passage]. Yesterday the seventh class was being examined.

o: XIX Cal. Jan. Nundinae annuae heri inchoatae, quibus res donandae natis festo die, quo Christi nativitas in memoriam revocatur, venum prostant. Heri praesertim, quo die e rure homines frequentissime adsunt, videres vino titubantes per vias bacchari, quorum unusquisque calceos aut alia vel sibi vel uxori vel natis emerat; videres [p. 441] innumeros hic lites agitari, illis merces licitari et alia multa. - Feriae nobis erant duobus his diebus, quorum primo dimidio negotia faciundo, reliquo tempore otia, jocos, discursitationes et ambulationes celebravi. Incumbit jam in me onus, fausta cuivis professorum precandi Jani Calendis, cui quidem negotio veteres praesertim medii aevi Latini poetae egregium praestant et praestiterunt auxilium. XVIII Cal. Jan. Per semestre hoc hibernum placet jam, doctore et fautore maxime venerando Domino Hopfio praesertim suasore, Latina sumere et in his praecipue elaborare. Vacillor autem et in varias partes trahor, quo potissimum classico auctore uterer? Occurrerunt Ciceronis quaestiones Tusculanae, quas et Germanas facere et illustrare institui. Sed quae juvenilis est inconstantia, displicet jam consilium, si minus per Latinitatis obscuritatem et difficultatem, quae abest longissime ab hoc opere, per philosophiam et eloquentiam, quas potissimum, ut ipse ait, hic adhibere visum est. XVII Cal. Jan. Nox erat et tranquilla mente libello cuidam obsidebam, cum flagrare in urbe nostra aedem sonitus campanae nos exterreret. Heu, quantus omnes invasit metus! Invalescente jam incendio, ego meusque pater auxilium ivimus domui cuidam vicinitatis. Ibi vero videres aedem flagrantem totam igne et paene jam incendio consumtam. Domum illam cum pervenissemus, senescere jam coepit flamma et paullo post evanescere paene et fumum late tolli ad astra. Quid plura? Hora vix elapsa restincta est flamma, consumta domus dimidia. XVI Cal. Jan. Causam vero, quae incendium commoverit, sexcenties variant. Narrant plerique, plumbo, quod ajunt, infuso. Sed et hic differunt alii. Quid tamen recensio tot rumorum proficiat?. Consentiunt vero plerique, filiae Praeceptoris ineptias nugasque et aetate et ordine indignissimas igni fuisse causam, quae quidem, dum salvare vellet lectum aliquem, valde et cripes et faciem et vestimenta cremata est. XII Cal. Jan. Bruma fuit hodie et dies S. Thomae festus. Jam jam gravissimum anni tempus cum sustinuerimus, id certe solatur, quod nunc dies in posterum magis magisque augeantur. Parvus etiam institutus est in nostra domo vocum nervorumque concentus, quo Dominus Oberst de Rau, inhabitans superiorem nostrae aedis partem, adfuit, quo digrediente venit Dom. Secret. Moser eiusque uxor, Dom. Secret. Günzler eiusdemque uxor et Dom. Zoror, frater duarum uxorum.
e: [Latin] The 19th day before the Calends of January. The annual fair began yesterday, at which things to be given to children on the festal day on which the nativity of Christ is recalled are offered for sale. Yesterday especially, the day on which men from the country are present in greatest numbers, you could see them reeling with wine and revelling through the streets, each of whom had bought shoes or other things either for himself or for his wife or for his children; you could see [p. 441] countless disputes being waged here, wares being haggled over there, and many other things. — We had a holiday on these two days, of which I spent the first half in transacting business, the remaining time I devoted to leisure, jests, running about and walks. The burden now lies upon me of praying auspicious things for each of the professors on the Calends of Janus, in which task the old Latin poets, especially of the Middle Ages, provide and have provided excellent help. [Latin] The 18th day before the Calends of January. For this winter semester I am pleased now, with my most venerable teacher and patron Herr Hopf especially as adviser, to take up Latin things and to work on these especially. But I vacillate and am drawn in various directions as to which classical author I should use above all. There occurred to me Cicero’s Tusculan Questions, which I resolved both to make German and to illustrate. But, such is juvenile inconstancy, my plan now displeases me, if less on account of the obscurity and difficulty of the Latinity, which is very far from this work, than on account of philosophy and eloquence, which, as he himself says, it seemed best to employ here. [Latin] The 17th day before the Calends of January. It was night and, with a tranquil mind, I was sitting over a certain little book when the sound of bells, that a house in our city was burning, terrified us. Alas, what fear seized all! As the fire was already gaining strength, I and my father went to the aid of a certain house in the neighborhood. There you could see the house blazing all over with fire and almost already consumed by the conflagration. When we had come to that house, the flame began to die down and a little later almost to vanish, and the smoke to be borne far up to the stars. What more? Scarcely an hour had passed when the flame was extinguished, half the house consumed. [Latin] The 16th day before the Calends of January. The cause, however, which started the fire, they vary six hundred times. Most narrate that it was lead, as they say, poured in. But here too others differ. Yet what would the review of so many rumors accomplish? Most agree, however, that the follies and trifles of the preceptor’s daughter, most unworthy of her age and station, were the cause of the fire; who, while she wished to save a certain bed, was badly burned in hair, face and clothing. [Latin] The 12th day before the Calends of January. It was the winter solstice today and the feast day of St. Thomas. Now that we have borne the heaviest time of the year, this at least consoles, that now the days will be increased more and more in future. A small concert of voices and strings was also arranged in our house, at which Colonel de Rau, who lives in the upper part of our house, was present; when he departed there came Secretary Moser and his wife, Secretary Günzler and his wife, and Herr Zoror, brother of the two wives.

o: XI Cal. Jan. Jam dudum equidem antea, quam gravi morbo implicarer, quae consequuta sunt et mala et bona perturbationum animi, explicare pro mei ingenii modulo incepi. Quae honoris, jam exposui. Multa quoque bona sequuta esse, nemo negaverit, si homini, qui captus ea libidine fuit, quaesivit honorem ex bene factis. Ubiquidem facta rectissima, consilia vero, si per honorem capta sint, minus probe dixeris. Recte enim facta, ubi virtute perpetrentur, non lucri sui cupidine, ea maxime sunt laudanda. X Cal. Jan. Ordiamur jam auri opumque libidinem, quae sive sordida avaritia est, sive dehonestans pecuniae injuria quaerendae cupido. Quod si prior, quam dixi, avaritia, occupaverit animum, aliis minus, quam sibi ipse nocet. Hominum est infelicissimus etc. Die Schilderung schließt endlich mit der Bemerkung, daß der Geizige auch gegen seine Familie und Diener treulos, grausam sein müsse; maxima tamen fraus, si principis fuerit minister, in dominum, cui fidum esse vel juramento se obstrinxit. VIII Cal. Jan. Die Solis. Dies hodie beatissimo nostro servatori festus obortus est, ubi ex more et ego lautissimis a patre muneribus sum affectus, quorum quidem cum sint multa gratissima, jucundissimum tamen utilissimumque est Schelleri Lexicon, cujus praestantiam usu saepius ipse jam percepi. Ipsis Cal. Jan. 1786. Novus igitur sub DEI auspiciis annus inluxit. Mediis his diebus emi mihi etiam Schelleri praecepta styli bene Latini imprimis Ciceroniani. III Id. Febr. 1786. Redeamus jam ad prisca haec nostra stylo exercendo instituta, intermissa longo intervallo temporis, cum sit hodie Serenissimi Domini nostri Ducis natalis LIXtus Nescio quo casu concionem, qua explicabatur Cap. IX Sapientiae Salomonis, nullam adivi. Post meridiem audivi orationem in Gymnasio Dom. Prof. Schmidtii, quae egit de meritis nostri Ducis de re litteraria Wirtembergiue et quidem exposuit excellentia, quae de Tubingensi studiorum Universitate demeritus erat; deinde, quae de nostro Gymnasio, postea de scholis claustralibus; sequebantur scholae triviales et quas vocant Germanae; excepit has splendida institutio Academiae primo quidem militaris, insequenti tempore complexu hujus instituti amplificato, et literariae; addidit denique et institutum sexui sequiori consulendo, quam vocant scholam, école. Clausit totam orationem ardentibus pro salute Ducis nostri eiusque maritae nunc peregrinantium votis precibusque.
e: [Latin] The 11th day before the Calends of January. Long since, indeed, before I was entangled in a grave illness, I began, so far as my modest talent allows, to explain the evils and goods that followed from the perturbations of the mind. Those of honor I have already set out. That many good things too followed, no one will deny, if the man who was seized by that desire sought honor from good deeds. Wherever indeed the deeds are most upright, the plans, however, if adopted through honor, you would call less upright. For right deeds, when they are accomplished from virtue, not from desire for one’s own gain, are most of all to be praised. [Latin] The 10th day before the Calends of January. Let us now begin with the desire for gold and wealth, which is either sordid avarice or a dishonoring desire of acquiring money by injustice. But if the former, which I have called avarice, has taken hold of the mind, it harms others less than himself. He is the most unhappy of men, etc. The description concludes finally with the remark that the miser must also be faithless and cruel toward his own family and servants; [Latin] yet the greatest fraud, if he is a prince’s minister, is against the master to whom he has bound himself even by oath to be faithful. [Latin] The 8th day before the Calends of January. Sunday. A day festal for our most blessed Savior has arisen today, on which, as is the custom, I too was favored by my father with most splendid gifts; of which, although many are most welcome, the most pleasant and useful is Scheller’s Lexicon, whose excellence I have already myself often perceived by use. [Latin] On the Calends of January itself, 1786. The new year has thus dawned under the auspices of GOD. In the midst of these days I bought for myself also Scheller’s precepts of good Latin style, above all the Ciceronian. [Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of February, 1786. Let us now return to these our earlier exercises for practicing style, interrupted for a long interval of time, since today is the fifty-ninth birthday of our Most Serene Lord the Duke. By what chance I know not, I attended no sermon in which Chapter IX of the Wisdom of Solomon was expounded. In the afternoon I heard in the Gymnasium an oration of Professor Schmidt, which dealt with the merits of our Duke toward literary affairs of Württemberg and indeed expounded the excellences in which he had deserved well of the University of Tübingen; then those toward our Gymnasium, afterwards toward the cloister schools; there followed the trivial schools and those they call German ones; these were succeeded by the splendid institution of the Academy, at first indeed military, afterwards, the scope of this institution having been enlarged, also literary; he added finally also an institution for providing for the weaker sex, which they call a school, école. He closed the whole oration with ardent vows and prayers for the welfare of our Duke and his consort, now traveling.

o: Obschon Hegel mit dieser Uebersicht aller damaligen Bildungsanstalten Würtembergs einen neuen Anlauf nahm, seinen Lateinischen Styl durch den Anreiz eines Tagebuchs unaufhörlich zu üben und zu verbessern, so muß es ihm doch entweder an erregsamem Stoff zu Aufzeichnungen gefehlt oder sein Eifer durch hinreichenden Erfolg sich befriedigt gesehen haben. Es kommen von jekt ab nur noch einige allgemeinere Betrachtungen in Lateinischer Sprache vor. Die eine derselben aus dem März 1786 enthält das Brouillon zu einer Lateinischen Rede über die Geselligkeit, welche er auf dem Gymnasium im Lauf des Sommers halten wollte, wenn die Reihe solcher rhetorischen Uebung an ihn käme. Er legt es dabei darauf an, in der Anordnung so schulgerecht als möglich zu Werke zu gehen und in der Ausführung alle traditionellen Schmuckphrasen und für Ciceronianisch gehaltenen Uebergangswendungen anzubringen. Es würde ermüdend sein, das Ganze mitzutheilen; einige Puncte jedoch, über den Vortheil, welchen der Umgang mit älteren Personen darbietet, über die Nothwendigkeit der Beobachtung der geselligen Formen, über die Grenzen der Geselligkeit und über den Umgang mit dem schwächeren Geschlecht sind zu charakteristisch für Hegel selbst, als daß sie nicht ausgehoben zu werden verdienten. Uebrigens ist das Latein wirklich nur Brouillonlatein:
e: Although Hegel, with this survey of all the educational institutions then existing in Württemberg, made a new start at practicing and improving his Latin style incessantly through the stimulus of a diary, he must nevertheless either have lacked stimulating material for entries or have seen his zeal satisfied by adequate success. From now on there occur only a few more general reflections in the Latin language. One of them, from March 1786, contains the rough draft of a Latin speech on sociability, which he wished to deliver at the Gymnasium in the course of the summer, when the turn for such rhetorical exercise should come to him. He aims thereby to proceed as scholastically correct as possible in the arrangement and to bring in, in the execution, all the traditional ornamental phrases and transitional turns held to be Ciceronian. It would be tiresome to communicate the whole; but some points, on the advantage which association with older persons offers, on the necessity of observing the social forms, on the limits of sociability and on association with the weaker sex, are too characteristic of Hegel himself for them not to deserve being extracted. Moreover the Latin is really only rough-draft Latin:

o: „Primum ergo et potissimum cum natu majoribus conversatis redundat commodum, quod multas rerum multarum notitias sibi comparent. Accedit imprimis notitia, quae nulli vel aliquo cum fructu in aliorum salute laboranti, vel se ipse non velit riteorbi committere cum summo detrimento, haec est notitia hominum. Addamus, qua re in nostris temporibus moribusque praesertim supersederi nequit, ritus quosdam et externa specie formaque se commendandi facillime discet, qui versatus fuerit diu in hominibus politis cultisque et moribus; ut ita dicam, longa cum mundo consuetudine tritus. Cum, qui ab externa parte non nitet, et eadem animi stupiditate laborare creditur. Cum tanta igitur fluant e consuetudine justa cum aliis hominibus, necesse est, ex perversa et nimi, si ita dicere fas est, multa scaturire mala. Quae sunt: a. animi dissipatio et distractio; b. amissio temporis; c. alienatio etfastidium ab omni re, severiorem animum poscente et ab solitudine. Venio jam ad consuetudinem sexus sequioris, quo quidem scopulo multi et praeclarissimi animo misere perierunt. Quid ergo faciendum? Abstinendum omni plane cum illis commercio? Nati sumus, ut dixi, ea lege, qui commercium et consuetudinem colamus. At feminae non sunt homines? Quis hoc contendet? Utendum igitur est illis. Sed quaeritur, quae et quantae ca [p. 444] lamitates consequantur? Caret consuetudo illa omnibus commodis? Absit! Immo, si recte utaris, maxima tibi offeret. Qui enim, quod sane quisque Vestrûm et volet et velit, hos inter homines, qui nunc globum tuentur, fortunatus cupit esse, eum abjicere necesse est, ut ita dicam: Schlacken, quod nusquam melius et diligentius fieri poterit, quam in societate illarum. Habent enim laudisque infamiaeque monopolium! " Eine wichtige Reflexion enthält eine andere Stelle des Tagebuchs aus demselben Monat. Hegel vergleicht darin die Religion des Ethnicismus mit dem gewöhnlichen christlichen Glauben. Da die Schriftsteller der Alten eine so reiche Quelle intellectueller und sittlicher Bildung für ihn waren, so stieß er sich an der wegwerfenden Weise, mit welcher Viele die Alten ihrer Religion wegen behandelten. Er fand aus, daß, was man ihnen als Aberglauben zurechne, denen selbst nicht fremd sei, welche solche Vorwürfe machten. Er überzeugte sich, daß der Glaube an Engel und Teufel nur eine Wiederholung des antiken Dämonenglaubens sei. Er verabscheute die Consequenzen, welche aus einer solchen Vorstellung für die Freiheit des Menschen sich ergeben müssen. Er erkannte die göttliche Würde des Menschen darin, daß er für seine guten und bösen Thaten selbst verantwortlich sei.
e: “[Latin] First, then, and foremost, there accrues to those who converse with their elders the advantage that they procure for themselves the knowledge of many things. To this is added, above all, a knowledge which no one, whether he labors with some fruit for the welfare of others or does not wish to commit himself properly to the world, [can lack] without the greatest detriment — this is the knowledge of men. Let us add — a thing which in our times and customs especially cannot be dispensed with — that he will most easily learn certain rites and the art of commending oneself by outward appearance and form who has long been versed among polished and cultivated men and manners; worn, so to speak, by long familiarity with the world. For he who does not shine on the outward side is believed to labor under the same dullness of mind. — Since, then, so many benefits flow from just intercourse with other men, it is necessary that from a perverse and excessive [intercourse], if one may so say, many evils spring forth. These are: a. dissipation and distraction of the mind; b. loss of time; c. alienation and distaste for everything that requires a more serious mind, and for solitude. — I come now to the intercourse of the weaker sex, a reef on which many, and the most distinguished in spirit, have miserably perished. What then is to be done? Must one abstain wholly from any commerce with them? We are born, as I said, under the law that we cultivate commerce and intercourse. But are women not human beings? Who will contend this? We must therefore use them. But it is asked what and how great calamities [p. 444] follow? Is that intercourse devoid of all advantages? Far from it! On the contrary, if you use it rightly, it will offer you the greatest. For he who, as surely each of you both wants and would want, desires to be fortunate among the men who now inhabit the globe, must cast off, so to speak: Schlacken [dross], which nowhere can be done better and more diligently than in the society of these women. For they have the monopoly of praise and of infamy!” An important reflection is contained in another passage of the diary from the same month. Hegel compares therein the religion of heathenism with the ordinary Christian faith. Since the writers of the ancients were such a rich source of intellectual and ethical culture for him, he took offense at the disparaging manner in which many treated the ancients on account of their religion. He found that what is charged against them as superstition is not alien to those themselves who made such reproaches. He convinced himself that the belief in angels and devils is only a repetition of the antique belief in demons. He abhorred the consequences which must result from such a representation for the freedom of man. He recognized the divine dignity of man in this, that he is himself responsible for his good and evil deeds.

o: V Id. Martii 1786. Saepe mihi de collustratis nostris temporibus cogitanti incurrit et in animum, saepe a nobis convicia et illusiones jaci in varios errores paganorum et omnino in omnium priscorum mores et vetustate firmatas opiniones. Quae nunc de illis recurrent menti, paucis calamo mandabo. In explicanda Deûm historia universaque mythologia audivi, cum illuderetur priscis, de superstitione ipsorum, quippe qui duos sibi praeesse credebant genios, alterum bonum, alterum malum, hos perpetua concertatione congredi, quorum si bonus malum superaret, bene ab homine et cogitari et agi; si contra vinceret malus hominemque dominaretur, prava et menti occurrere et in prave acta erumpere hominem. Deliberans, an eadem nostri aevi tenerentur opinione, inveni, plurimos omnia bene cogitata et facta divinis viribus, prave viribus diaboli adsignare. Parum differre inter se has utriusque aevi opiniones quisque viderit. Accedit quamvis unus diabolus toti generi humano, unicuique et singulo insidiari semper dicatur, id tamen auget similitudinem, quod unus homo probus unum pluresve habere angelos, vitae suae morumque custodes, qui recedant ab hominibus pravis, creditur. Si quis forsan homo ex plebe commisit aliquid contra leges, hoc suam culpam diluere aliqua ex parte putant, quod Deum dicant ab ipso cessisse passumque esse, ut cade [p. 445] ret. At id est divinae bonitatis providentia. Est quidem, at repugnaret consilio, quo homines formavit. Voluit enim non deficere aliquod in rerum universi catena membrum, quod esset inter bestias, quo ferreis instincti vinculis coacti, libertate carentes, bonum an malum eligant, suo nihil consilio faciunt, et inter aethereum illud angelorum genus, qui ab omni malo alieni nonnisi recta perficiunt. Relictus est igitur homini medius inter hos locus, cujus plane arbitrio datum, utrum bonum an malum eligat. Simili errore multos e Christianis irridere vidi. Crediderunt quippe pagani pacari Deûm iras jejuniis, cibis potuque Deo appositis. Referamus id ad nostra tempora. Multis in ritibus eandem adhuc durare superstitionem vidi, ut in sepulchralibus aliisque apud collustratiores Lutheranos. Ast apud Catholicos totus ad hanc diem viget. Hoc solo differunt. Pagani apposuere ipsis Diis cibos suos; quos si sacerdotes devoraverint, a Diis esse comestos putaverunt. Hodie non item. Superstitiosi enim hi homunciones pecuniam, alimenta atque alia tradunt sacerdotibus eoque gratiam Dei aucupant. Sed quae major, quae horribilior superstitio stultitia fuit? Am 18. März folgt eine moralische Betrachtung über den Zorn, welchen Hegel auch in Ansehung von Schandthaten nicht zugeben will: non necesse est, in iram abripi; satis est, dolere de sceleribus aegreque ea ferre. Endlich am 22. März schließt er: si quis tam adeo sibi imperare didicit -, ut nulla re in iram moveatur, ei liceat, succensere sceleribus! Unmittelbar darauf schreibt er: „Alle Menschen haben die Absicht, sich glücklich zu machen, mit einigen seltenen Ausnahmen, die, um Andere glücklich zu machen, so viel Erhabenheit der Seele besaßen, sich aufzuopfern. Doch diese haben, glaub ' ich, nicht wahre Glückseligkeit aufgeopfert, sondern nur zeitliche Vortheile, zeitliches Glück, auch Leben. Diese machen also hier noch keine Ausnahme. " Dann folgt noch ohne Anfang und Ende ein Fragment über die Aufklärung durch Wissenschaft und Kunst, aus welchem folgende Bemerkungen nicht übergangen werden dürfen: „Einen Entwurf von einer Aufklärung des gemeinen Mannes zu machen, halte ich theils für die meisten auch gelehrtesten Leute sehr schwer, theils aber auch besonders für mich viel schwerer, da ich überhaupt die Geschichte noch nicht philosophisch und gründlich studirt habe. Sonst glaube ich auch, diese Aufklärung des gemeinen Mannes habe sich immer nach der Religion seiner Zeit gerichtet. -- In Ansehung der Wissenschaften und Künste bin ich also der Meinung, sie haben zuerst im Orient geblüht und seien dann von da aus immer mehr nach Westen gewandert.
e: [Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of March, 1786. Often, as I think about our enlightened times, it also occurs to my mind that reproaches and mockeries are often hurled by us against the various errors of the pagans and in general against the customs of all the ancients and the opinions confirmed by antiquity. What now recurs to my mind concerning them I shall commit to the pen in a few words. In the explanation of the history of the Gods and of mythology as a whole I heard, when the ancients were being mocked, about their superstition, since they believed that two genii presided over them, one good, the other evil; that these meet in perpetual conflict; and that if the good overcame the evil, things are well thought and done by man; if on the contrary the evil conquered and dominated man, depraved things both occur to the mind and the man breaks forth into wickedly done acts. Deliberating whether the opinion of our own age were the same, I found that very many assign all things well thought and done to divine powers, wickedly done to the powers of the devil. Everyone will see that these opinions of the two ages differ little from one another. Add that, although one devil is said always to lie in wait for the whole human race and for each single one, yet this increases the similarity, that one upright man is believed to have one or more angels, guardians of his life and morals, who withdraw from wicked men. If perchance some man of the common people has committed something against the laws, they think to wash away his guilt in some part by this, that they say God withdrew from him and permitted that he should fall, [p. 445] But that is the providence of divine goodness. It is indeed, but it would conflict with the design by which He formed men. For He willed that there should not be lacking in the chain of the universe of things a certain link, which should stand between the beasts — who, compelled by the iron bonds of instinct and lacking the liberty [to decide] whether they choose good or evil, do nothing by their own counsel — and that ethereal race of angels, who, alien to all evil, accomplish only what is right. There was left therefore to man the middle place between these, to whose entire discretion it is given whether he choose good or evil. I have seen many of the Christians deride a like error. For the pagans believed that the wrath of the Gods is appeased by fasts, and by food and drink set before God. Let us refer this to our own times. In many rites I have seen the same superstition still persist, as in funeral rites and others among the more enlightened Lutherans. But among the Catholics it flourishes entire to this day. In this alone they differ. The pagans set their own foods before the Gods themselves; if the priests devoured them, they thought they had been eaten by the Gods. Today it is not so. For these superstitious little men hand over money, victuals and other things to the priests and thereby hunt after the favor of God. But what greater, what more horrible superstition or folly has there been? On 18 March there follows a moral reflection on anger, which Hegel does not wish to admit even in regard to infamous deeds: [Latin] it is not necessary to be carried away into anger; it is enough to grieve over crimes and to bear them with distress. Finally on 22 March he concludes: [Latin] if anyone has learned so far to command himself that he is moved to anger by nothing, let him be permitted to be angry at crimes! — Immediately afterward he writes: “All human beings have the intention of making themselves happy, with a few rare exceptions who, in order to make others happy, possessed so much sublimity of soul as to sacrifice themselves. Yet these, I believe, have not sacrificed true blessedness, but only temporal advantages, temporal happiness, also life. These therefore make no exception here.” — Then there follows, without beginning and end, a fragment on enlightenment through science and art, from which the following remarks must not be passed over: “To make a draft of an enlightenment of the common man I hold partly for most, even the most learned people, very difficult, partly however also especially for me much harder, since I have in general not yet studied history philosophically and thoroughly. Otherwise I believe that this enlightenment of the common man has always oriented itself according to the religion of its time. — With regard to the sciences and arts I am therefore of the opinion that they flourished first in the Orient and then migrated from there more and more toward the West.

o: So sehr man nun heut zu Tage, wenigstens in Betreff der Philosophie, das große Rühmen von der Gelehrsamkeit der Aegyptier mit Recht vermeidet, so bleibt doch so viel gewiß, daß sie es wenigstens in Ansehung der mechanischen und bildenden Künste zu einem solchen Grad der Vollkommenheit gebracht haben, daß noch jest die Trümmer ihrer Kunstwerke bewundert werden, und es ist sehr wahrscheinlich, daß die großen und weitläuftigen praktischen - Kenntnisse auch schon in eine genauere Theorie gebracht worden seien. " Weiter findet sich nichts aus dem Jahre 1786. Mit den ersten Tagen des nächsten Jahres sekt er noch einmal zu einem Tagebuch an, hält es aber nur eine Woche lang aus. Um so nothwendiger wird die Mittheilung dieser Selbstschilderung sein. Eine noch entschiedenere Selbstständigkeit, etwa abgerechnet, findet sich im Wesen keine Veränderung. Es ist immer das Streben nach wissenschaftlicher Ausbildung im Vordergrunde; daneben ergreift die Reflexion aber auch, was von dem allgemeinen Leben sich Interessantes darbietet; an sich selbst denkt er am wenigsten. Seine einzige durchgreifende Eigenheit ist die Selbstlosigkeit der objectivsten Sinnesart.
e: Much as one nowadays, at least in respect of philosophy, rightly avoids the great praise of the learning of the Egyptians, so much at least remains certain, that in regard to the mechanical and the fine arts they brought themselves to such a degree of perfection that even now the ruins of their works of art are admired; and it is very probable that the great and extensive practical knowledge had also already been brought into a more exact theory.” — Nothing further is found from the year 1786. With the first days of the next year he sets about a diary once more, but keeps it up for only a week. All the more necessary will be the communication of this self-portrayal. Apart perhaps from a still more decided independence, no change is to be found in his nature. The striving for scientific cultivation is always in the foreground; alongside it, however, reflection also seizes upon whatever of interest the general life presents; of himself he thinks least. His one pervasive peculiarity is the selflessness of the most objective cast of mind.

o: Am 1. Januar 1787. Gegenwärtig bin ich das erste Jahr in der siebenten Classe des hiesigen Gymnasiums. Mein Hauptaugenmerk sind noch immer die Sprachen und zwar wirklich die Griechische und Lateinische. Daneben arbeite ich zuweilen etwas in der Mathematik. Außer den öffentlichen Lectionen höre ich ein Collegium bei Herrn Prof. Hopf, worin wir 3 Stunden dem Longin und eine Stunde den Pflichten des Cicero widmen. Von der Art, wie wir sie lesen, ist unnöthig, etwas zu sagen. Einige Zeit wende ich auch auf Ausarbeitung kleiner Aufsäße und Niederschreibung meiner Gedanken. Sonntags arbeite ich meist in der sphärischen Trigonometrie und zum Theil widme ich ihn guten Freunden. Uebrige Viertelstunden fülle ich wirklich mit Lesung und Excerpirung der Excurse Heyne's zu seinem Virgil aus. Den Vormittag fing ich an, in der sphärischen Trigonometrie, die ich aus Lorenzen's Mathematik abgeschrieben hatte, etwas durchzugehen. Allein ich wurde durch Visiten, die zu Neujahr Glück wünschten, bald unterbrochen und nachher mußte ich in gleichen Angelegenheiten ausgehen. Den Nachmittag wollte ich nur Einiges in Sophiens Reise lesen, ich konnte mich aber nimmer davon losreißen bis an den Abend, wo ich in das Concert ging. Es ist nämlich gewöhnlich, daß alle Neujahr Deputirte von Eflingen dem Herzog unter dem Titel Schusgeld 100 Ducaten überreichen, worauf denn allemal in der Akademie ein Concert veranstaltet wird. Von diesem konnte man zwar we [p. 447] gen dem Getose der vielen Zuhörer wenig hören, allein die Zeit wurde mir doch sehr angenehm verkürzt, indem ich da gute Freunde sprach, die ich schon lange nimmer gesehen hatte. Das Anschauen schöner Mädchen trug zu unserer Unterhaltung auch nicht wenig bei. Dienstag den 2. Januar. Gewöhnlich; ich excerpirte Abends aus Heyne's Ercursen. Mittwoch den 3. Ianuar. Es war diese Nacht eine totale Mondfinsterniß. Herr Prof. Hopf rüstete auf dem Gymnasio einige Sehrohre zur Beobachtung aus dem neuen Apparat der Instrumente. Es kamen Einige, aber der ganz überzogene Himmel ließ nicht das Mindeste sehen. Herr Rector, illuminirt, erzählte uns unter Anderem: er sei auch als Gymnasiast mit Andern Observator gewesen und des Nachts stellatum gegangen. Sie seien aber nur herumvagirt. Es kamen Stadtphilister dazu, die sie einziehen wollten. Die Gymnasiasten sagten: sie seien stellatum gegangen. Ei, sagten die Soldaten, sie sollten bei Nacht in ihren Betten liegen und bei Tag stellatum gehen. Donnerstag den 4. Januar. 1-2 besuchte ich Haug, Sohn des Hofinstrumentenmachers allhier, woich eine Uhr sah, die vortrefflich in dem Ton einer Queerflöte spielte. 4-5 und 6-7 excerpirte ich aus Heyne's Excursen; sonst ging Alles gewöhnlich. Freitags den 5. Ianuar. Von 9-10 excerpirte ich aus einem Theil der Allgemeinen Deutschen Bibliothek die Editionen des Demosthenes. Von 10-11 besuchte ich Griesinger, den Sohn des Herrn Consistorialraths. Ich sah dort den Atlas coelestis von Mayer und die sämmtliche Bibliothek des Herrn Consistorialraths: auch entlehnte ich daraus den zweiten Theil von Kästner's Mathematik. Nachmittags las und excerpirte ich aus einem Theil der Allgemeinen Deutschen Bibliothek. 5-6 war Collegium im Longin wegen dem Feiertag am folgenden Tag. Nach dem Essen las ich in Kästner's Mathematik.
e: On 1 January 1787. At present I am in the first year in the seventh class of the local Gymnasium. My chief concerns are still the languages, and indeed really Greek and Latin. Besides that I work now and then a little in mathematics. Apart from the public lessons I attend a lecture course with Professor Hopf, in which we devote 3 hours to Longinus and one hour to the Duties of Cicero. Of the manner in which we read them it is unnecessary to say anything. Some time I also give to the working out of small essays and to writing down my thoughts. On Sundays I work mostly at spherical trigonometry, and in part I devote them to good friends. Remaining quarter-hours I really fill out with reading and excerpting Heyne’s excursuses to his Virgil. In the forenoon I began to go through a little of the spherical trigonometry that I had copied out of Lorentzen’s Mathematics. But I was soon interrupted by visits that came to wish a happy New Year, and afterwards I had to go out on like errands. In the afternoon I meant only to read a little in Sophie’s Journey, but I could never tear myself away from it until the evening, when I went to the concert. For it is the custom that every New Year deputies from Esslingen present the Duke, under the title of protection money, with 100 ducats, whereupon each time a concert is arranged in the Academy. Of this one could, to be sure, hear little because of [p. 447] the din of the many listeners, but the time was nevertheless made very pleasantly short for me by my speaking there with good friends whom I had not seen for a long time. The sight of beautiful girls also contributed not a little to our conversation. Tuesday, the 2nd of January. As usual; in the evening I excerpted from Heyne’s excursuses. Wednesday, the 3rd of January. This night there was a total lunar eclipse. Professor Hopf equipped some telescopes at the Gymnasium for observation, from the new apparatus of instruments. Some came, but the completely overcast sky did not let one see the least thing. The Rector, illuminated [tipsy], told us among other things: he too, as a Gymnasium pupil, had been an observer with others and had gone stellatum by night. They had only been roaming about. Town philistines came along, who wanted to haul them in. The Gymnasium pupils said: they had gone stellatum. Oh, said the soldiers, they should lie in their beds by night and go stellatum by day. Thursday, the 4th of January. 1–2 I visited Haug, son of the court instrument-maker here, where I saw a clock that played excellently in the tone of a transverse flute. — 4–5 and 6–7 I excerpted from Heyne’s excursuses; otherwise everything went as usual. Friday, the 5th of January. From 9 to 10 I excerpted from a part of the Allgemeine Deutsche Bibliothek [General German Library] the editions of Demosthenes. From 10 to 11 I visited Griesinger, the son of the consistory councillor. There I saw the Atlas coelestis [celestial atlas] of Mayer and the whole library of the consistory councillor; I also borrowed from it the second part of Kästner’s Mathematics. In the afternoon I read and excerpted from a part of the Allgemeine Deutsche Bibliothek. 5–6 there was a lecture course on Longinus, on account of the holiday on the following day. After dinner I read in Kästner’s Mathematics.

o: Samstag den 6. Januar. Den Vormittag bis halb eilf Uhr widmete ich der Trigonometrie. Nachher besuchte ich Herrn Prof. Hopf wegen einer dunklen Stelle in Kästner's Mathematik (II, 1765, р. 159). Ich war der Meinung, die Pole eines Kreises stehen immer um einen Quadranten von allen Puncten der Peripherie des Kreises. Aber daraus würde folgen, daß nur größte Kreise einer Kugel Pole haben könnten. Herr Prof. Hopf nahm selbst diesen Saz an. Erst nachher fiel mir aber der Irrthum ein und da schaffte ich mir selbst Rath. - Nachmittags besuchte ich Steinkopf, der seinem Großvater, dem Antiquar Betulius, der schon alt zu werden anfängt, überall recht gute Dienste [p. 448] leistet undvon seinen vielen beschwerlichen Arbeiten den größten Theil trägt. Abends spielten wir das geographische Kartenspiel, das beinahe einerlei mit dem Tarok ist, nur daß dieses mehrere Abwechslung und Strafenhat; jenes hat auch keine Taroke, keinen Skip, keinen Bagatt. Nach dem Essen studirte ich in der sphärischen Trigonometrie, die mir nimmer so schwer vorkommt, als sie erschien, so lang ich noch nichts darin gethan hatte. Sonntag den 7. Januar. Vormittags Trigonometrie. Nach dem Essen lockte mich der schöne Himmel zum Spazierengehen an. Ich folgte dem Reiz und machte mir eine gesunde stundenlange Bewegung. Auf dem Weg begegneten mir unzählige Fußgänger, Reiter und Fahrende. Abends besuchte ich Leypolden in der Akademie. Alle übrige Zeit Nachmittags und nach dem Nachtessen wandte ich auf die Trigonometrie. Arbeiten aus der Gymnasialzeit. 1. Ueber das Ercipiren. 2. Unterredung zwischen Dreien. 3. Von der Religion der Griechen und Römer. 4. Ueber einige charakteristischeUnterschiede der alten Dichter. Ueber das Ercipiren. März 1786. „Da das sogenannte Ercipiren, die Niederschreibung eines Themas in einer andern Sprache, als in der das Thema abgefaßt ist, von Vielen, theils Lehrern, theils Andern, auf der einen Seite heftig vertheidigt und beibehalten, auf der andern Seite aber von eben so Vielen verworfen und verbannt wird, so will ich die Gründe, die man zur Vertheidigung desselben vorzubringen pflegt, so weit meine Einsicht reicht, untersuchen.
e: Saturday, the 6th of January. The forenoon until half past ten I devoted to trigonometry. Afterwards I visited Professor Hopf on account of an obscure passage in Kästner’s Mathematics (II, 1765, p. 159). I was of the opinion that the poles of a circle always stand a quadrant away from all points of the circumference of the circle. But from that it would follow that only great circles of a sphere could have poles. Professor Hopf himself accepted this proposition. Only afterwards, however, did the error occur to me, and then I helped myself. — In the afternoon I visited Steinkopf, who renders his grandfather, the antiquary Betulius, who is beginning to grow old, quite good service everywhere [p. 448] and bears the greatest part of his many burdensome labors. — In the evening we played the geographical card game, which is almost the same as tarok, except that the latter has more variety and penalties; the former also has no tarocs, no Skiß, no Bagatt. — After dinner I studied spherical trigonometry, which no longer seems to me as hard as it appeared as long as I had not yet done anything in it. Sunday, the 7th of January. Forenoon trigonometry. After dinner the beautiful sky enticed me to go for a walk. I followed the attraction and took myself a healthy exercise of several hours. On the way I met countless pedestrians, riders, and travelers in carriages. In the evening I visited Leypold in the Academy. All the remaining time, in the afternoon and after supper, I devoted to trigonometry. II. 1. On Excipiring. 2. Conversation among Three. 3. On the Religion of the Greeks and Romans. 4. On Some Characteristic Differences of the Ancient Poets. March 1786. “Since the so-called excipiring, the writing down of a theme in a language other than the one in which the theme is composed, is on the one hand vigorously defended and retained by many, partly teachers, partly others, and on the other hand rejected and banished by just as many, I will, so far as my insight extends, examine the grounds that are usually advanced in its defense.

o: A. Habe ich von Einigen sagen gehört, man gelange dadurch zu einem leichten und fließenden Styl, da viele junge Leute bei Uebersezungen, zu denen sie Muße haben, sich versteigen und schwülstig werden. Dieser Grund mag für Viele einige Wahrscheinlichkeit haben. Und gewiß, man fällt beim Ercipiren nicht leicht in Schwulst. Allein man bedenke, ob dieses sogenannte fließende Latein, ob es wirklich so fließendes Latein ist. Ich verstehe nun unter diesem numeröses und periodi = [p. 449] sches, völlig nach der Natur, das nicht in's Gekünstelte und Schwülstige verfällt. Man übersehe nun alle Regeln einer numerösen, periodischen und simpeln Schreibart und überlege, ob auch der Geübteste sie beim Ercipiren beobachten könne. Man bedenke die völlige Ungleichheit der Deutschen und anderer Sprachen; man wird bei der Exception meistens Deutsche Constructionen, Verbindungsarten und die nämliche Folge der Säge in der excipirten Sprache antreffen. - Was ist dann aber Schuld, daß junge Leute in die Sucht verfallen, schwülstiges Latein zu schreiben? Unter vielen Ursachen ist vielleicht diese als die Urquelle zu merken, nämlich die Art, wie man die vortrefflichsten Schriften der Alten liest. Vermöge dieser sollte man glauben, sie nügen zu nichts, als ihre Sprache daraus zu lernen, und ihre Sprache wieder zu weiter nichts, als daß man sie eben könne. Denn man nimmt ganz allein und blos auf die Wörter und Phrasen, gar nicht auf den Geist und die Natur derselben Rücksicht. Von Sachen ist gar nicht die Rede. Liest man nun einen solchen Autor, so giebt es Viele, die fleißig jede Phrasis ausarbeiten, sie sei nun aus einem Schriftsteller, der ein Redner, cin Historiker oder ein Philosoph ist; er schreibe natürlich, gekünstelt, dunkel u.. s w. Alles wird durch einander gemengt. Eine rednerische Phrase, durch welche ein Subject um der Deutlichkeit, um der Antithese willen, um daraus einen Beweis herzuleiten, umschrieben worden ist, wird dann in einer historischen geringfügigen Materie angebracht. So steht Livius IV, 3, wo Canulejus das unbillige und ungerechte Betragen der Patricier gegen die Plebejer recht deutlich vorstellen will, da diese eben so wie jene Römische Bürger seien, die Umschreibung von Mitbürger: cives nos eorum esse, et si non easdem opes habere, eandem patriam incolere; und kurz vorher: indigni, qui una secum urbe intra eadem moenia incoleretis. Eben so die rednerische Umschreibung von: sie gönnen euch das Leben nicht: lucis vobis hujus partem, si liceat, adimant, quod spiratis, quod vocem mittitis, quod formas hominum habetis, indignantur, und so viele tausend andere. Nun hat man gesagt, diese Phrasen seien schön. Man lobt die jungen Leute, wenn sie viele im nächsten Exercitio anbringen und nun denken sie auf nichts mehr, als jedes einzelne Wort durch die größte Phrase zu umschreiben. Ob sie am rechten oder unrechten Orte stehe, auf das sieht man nicht, sondern man mißt sie nach der Länge. Die größten sind die besten und so entsteht Schwulst und Bombast. Das Natürliche und Aechte der Sprache wird ganz vernachläßigt.
e: A. I have heard some say that one attains by it an easy and flowing style, since many young people in translations, for which they have leisure, overreach themselves and become bombastic. This ground may have some probability for many. And certainly one does not easily fall into bombast in excipiring. But consider whether this so-called flowing Latin, whether it is really such flowing Latin. I understand by this a rhythmical and periodic [p. 449] style, wholly according to nature, which does not fall into the contrived and the bombastic. Now survey all the rules of a rhythmical, periodic, and simple manner of writing, and consider whether even the most practiced can observe them in excipiring. Consider the complete dissimilarity of German and other languages; in the excipiation one will for the most part find German constructions, connectives, and the very same sequence of sentences in the excipired language. — But what is to blame, then, that young people fall into the craving to write bombastic Latin? Among many causes this is perhaps to be noted as the original source, namely the manner in which one reads the most excellent writings of the ancients. By virtue of this one should believe that they are of use for nothing except to learn their language from them, and to learn their language again for nothing further except that one simply knows it. For one takes account quite solely and merely of the words and phrases, not at all of their spirit and nature. Of subject matter there is no talk at all. If one now reads such an author, there are many who diligently work up every phrase, be it from a writer who is an orator, a historian, or a philosopher; he may write naturally, artificially, obscurely, etc. Everything is mixed together. A rhetorical phrase by which a subject, for the sake of clarity, for the sake of antithesis, in order to derive a proof from it, has been circumscribed, is then brought into a historical, trifling matter. So it stands in Livy IV, 3, where Canuleius wants to represent quite clearly the unfair and unjust conduct of the patricians toward the plebeians, since these are just like those Roman citizens, the circumlocution for “fellow citizen”: [Latin] that we are their fellow citizens, and, though we do not have the same means, inhabit the same fatherland; and, shortly before: [Latin] unworthy that you should dwell with them in the same city within the same walls. Just so the rhetorical circumlocution for “they begrudge you life”: [Latin] they would take from you a share of this light, if they could; they are indignant that you breathe, that you utter a voice, that you have the forms of men — and so many thousand others. Now it has been said that these phrases are beautiful. The young people are praised when they bring in many of them in the next exercise, and now they think of nothing more than to circumscribe each single word by the greatest phrase. Whether it stands in the right or the wrong place, that is not looked to, but one measures it by length. The biggest are the best, and so arise bombast and fustian. The natural and genuine in the language is entirely neglected.

o: B. Man erlangt dadurch eine Fertigkeit, daß einem Worte und Redensarten geläufig werden und geschwind einfallen. Aber fragt es sich, ob durch ein solches Beeilen die Ueberlegung und die Wahl 29 der Worte [p. 450] nicht vielmehr gehindert werde. Bei bekannten Worten braucht es freilich nicht viel Nachdenken. Aber bei unbekanntern glaub ' ich es. Hat man die Phrasis oder das Wort noch nicht und es wird im Dictiren fortgefahren -, so soll man auch eilen. Man kann es aber nicht, man zittert und entweder läßt man einen leeren Play, oder man wird unwillig und im Unwillen ist man bekanntlich keiner Ueberlegung fähig Läßt man aber bei schweren Texten gar keine Lücke, so ist die Exception entweder gut oder schlecht. Ist sie gut, so hat man gewiß nicht durch's Excipiren, sondern öfteres Lesen der Quelle selbst und langsames Componiren diese Fertigkeit erlangt. Ist sie mittelmäßig oder schlecht, so sage man mir, zu was eine solche unselige Schreibseligkeit nüze? Es giebt Leute, die bei allen Fragen zu antworten wissen, wenn diese Antworten nur aus Worten bestehen, sie seien nun falsch, schaal oder übereilt, oder sogar ungereimt. So ist's beim Ercipiren, da ich hingegen den obigen diejenigen weit vorziehe, die zwar nicht sogleich, aber desto bedächtlicher und gescheuter antworten. Eben so gefällt mir beim Componiren eine kleine Langsamkeit besser, als beim Excipiren eine große Gile. Durch erstere wird unser Styl und die ganze Fertigkeit in einer Sprache reifer, überlegter und dem Geiste derselben mehr angemessen. Und durch des dächtliches Ueben gelangt man zu mehrer Schnelligkeit und endlich zu einer solchen, welche der beste Ercipist, der gleich Anfangs nie langsam gearbeitet hat, nie erreichen wird. Und diese besteht darin: schnell und zugleich gut zu schreiben.
e: B. One acquires by it a facility, so that words and expressions become familiar and occur quickly. But the question is whether by such hurrying the reflection and the choice of words [p. 450] are not rather hindered. With familiar words it indeed takes not much reflection. But with less familiar ones, I believe, it does. If one does not yet have the phrase or the word and the dictating goes on, one should hurry too. But one cannot, one falters, and — either one leaves a blank space, or one becomes unwilling, and in unwillingness one is notoriously incapable of reflection. But if with difficult texts one leaves no gap at all, then the excipiation is either good or bad. If it is good, then one has certainly acquired this facility not through excipiring, but through frequent reading of the source itself and slow composing. If it is mediocre or bad, then tell me, to what use is such a wretched scribbling mania? There are people who know how to answer all questions, if only these answers consist of words, be they false, shallow, or hasty, or even absurd. So it is in excipiring, whereas I far prefer to the above those who answer, to be sure, not at once, but all the more circumspectly and cleverly. Just so a little slowness in composing pleases me better than a great haste in excipiring. By the former our style and the whole facility in a language become riper, more considered, and more in keeping with its spirit. And through circumspect practice one attains to a greater speed, and finally to one such as the best excipist, who from the very beginning never worked slowly, will never reach. And this consists in this: writing quickly and at the same time well.

o: C. Aus dem Ercipiren, heißt es, kann man die Stärke in einer Sprache beurtheilen. Nun fragt sich, was für eine Stärke man darunter verstehe. Kann man kritische Stärke daraus ersehen? Wir wollen Gesner's Erklärung von der Kritik hier einsehen und dann urtheilen, ob man eine Stärke in ihr durch Ercipiren nicht erlange, sondern nur, ob sie sich ersehen lasse? Er erklärt sie nämlich als eine Fähigkeit zu urtheilen, die man durch den längsten Umgang mit den Alten erhält, nicht nur, was der Sinn der Worte sei, sondern hauptsächlich, ob ein ganzes Buch, eine ganze Abhandlung, eine Formel, ja sogar ein einzelnes Wort, wirklich von dem Alten herrühre, dem sie zugeschrieben werden. Man sieht gleich, daß diese Fertigkeit nicht die geringste Aehnlichkeit mit dem Excipiren habe und aus diesem beurtheilt werden könne. Ein guter Kritikus wird zwar immer die Worte und Redensarten gebrauchen, die das Dictirte eigentlich ausdrücken, aber der, welcher excipiren läßt, ist gemeiniglich ein schlechter oder gar kein Kritikus und kann eine solche Exception einer schlechtern aber phrasenreichern vorziehen. Doch dieser Fall gehört eigentlich gar nicht hieher, denn ein Kritikus ist [p. 451] kein Knabe, auch kein Jüngling mehr. Nein, das sind meistens erstarkte Männer unddiese wird man doch hoffentlich nicht nach dem Ercipiren beurtheilen. Eben so wenig, glaube ich, wird man die Stärke beurtheilen können, die man durch philosophisches Studium der Sprachen erlangt hat; oder die Stärke, die man in einer Sprache um des wahren Nuzens derselben, d. i. um sich Sachkenntnisse zu erwerben, erreicht hat. Doch auch zu dieser - Art gehört das, was wir von der vorhergehenden gesagt haben. Noch bleibt uns eine Art der Stärke in einer Sprache übrig. Es läßt sich nämlich noch aus dem Excipiren sehen, ob einer einen Vorrath von Wörtern sich gesammelt, ob er die Fertigkeit erworben hat, Deutschen Wörtern und Aufsäßen ein Lateinisches Kleid anzuziehen, das aber bei_weitem noch kein Römisches ist. Nun, dies will ich also zugeben und es ist wahr, aus dem Exponiren, wo der Context und der Vortheil, daß das Deutsche unsere Muttersprache ist, uns leichter die Bedeutung der Wörter in die Hand geben, kann man die Stärke in den Wörtern nicht so beurtheilen. Aber diese Stärke zu erlangen, wird gewiß das Ercipiren wenig behülflich sein. Wiederholtes Lesen der Bücher, die in dieser Sprache geschrieben sind, auch Ueberseven, sind hierzu die Mittel. Was ich hier überhaupt vom Excipiren gesagt habe, gilt von allen Arten des Ercipirens, vom Lateinischen, Deutschen u. s. f. Nur ist es bei einer Sprache menschlicher, als bei der andern, wo nämlich das Componiren noch Nuzen hat und welche noch wenigstens unter den Gelehrten eine lebende Sprache ist. Unterredung zwischen Dreien. 1785. 30. Mai. Antonius. Habt ihr über den Plan, den ich euch vorgelegt habe, nachgedacht? Seid ihr nunmehr schlüssig? Octavius. Ich habe ihn in Erwägung gezogen und wohl überlegt. Sollte die Ausführung so glücklich von Statten gehen, als der Plan weise und klug angeordnet ist, so wäre was Herrliches geschehen. Lepidus. Ich habe ihn eben so gefunden. Octavius. Aber wie? Nun wollen wir auch das Nähere davon bestimmen und den Hindernissen nachspüren, die sich uns in den Weg legen werden. Antonius. Ich habe nach langem Nachdenken keine besonderen Schwierigkeiten gefunden.
e: C. From excipiring, it is said, one can judge the strength in a language. Now the question is what kind of strength one understands by that. Can one see critical strength from it? Let us here look at Gesner’s explanation of criticism and then judge, not whether one acquires a strength in it through excipiring, but only whether it lets itself be seen from it? For he explains it as a faculty of judging, which one obtains through the longest intercourse with the ancients, not only what the sense of the words is, but chiefly whether a whole book, a whole treatise, a formula, indeed even a single word really comes from the ancient to whom it is ascribed. One sees at once that this facility has not the slightest similarity to excipiring and cannot be judged from it. A good critic will indeed always use the words and expressions that actually express what is dictated, but he who has excipiring done is commonly a bad critic or none at all, and can prefer to such an excipiation a worse but more phrase-rich one. Yet this case really does not belong here, for a critic is [p. 451] no boy, and no youth any more. No, they are mostly grown men, and these one will hopefully not judge by excipiring. — Just as little, I believe, will one be able to judge the strength that one has acquired through philosophical study of languages, or the strength that one has attained in a language for the sake of its true utility, i.e. in order to acquire factual knowledge. Yet to this kind too belongs what we said of the preceding. — There remains to us still one kind of strength in a language. For it can still be seen from excipiring whether someone has gathered a store of words, whether he has acquired the facility of putting a Latin garment on German words and sentences, which is, however, by far not yet a Roman one. Now, this I will grant, and it is true; since from construing, where the context and the advantage that German is our mother tongue more readily put the meaning of the words into our hands, one cannot so judge the strength in the words. But to acquire this strength excipiring will certainly be of little help. Repeated reading of the books written in this language, also translating, are the means for this. What I have said here in general about excipiring holds of all kinds of excipiring, from Latin, German, etc. Only it is more humane in the one language than in the other, namely where composing still has use and which is, at least among the learned, still a living language. 1785. 30 May. Antonius. Have you thought over the plan which I laid before you? Are you now resolved? Octavius. I have taken it into consideration and pondered it well. Should the execution proceed as happily as the plan is wisely and cleverly arranged, something glorious would come to pass. Lepidus. I have found it just so. Octavius. But how? Now let us also determine the details of it and trace out the hindrances that will lie in our way. Antonius. After long reflection I have found no particular difficulties.

o: Octavius. Aber ich. Ich will dir sie vorlegen. Werden sich die 29 * [p. 452] freien Römer so zu unserer Herrschaft verstehen? Wird Brutus, wird Cassius, werden die Andern, die den edlen Cäsar tödten halfen, stille dabei sein? Wird Sertus Pompejus sich zufrieden stellen lassen? Antonius. O! Octavius, keine solche Bedenklichkeiten! Glaube mir, ich habe länger in der Welt gelebt, habe mehr Erfahrung, als du. Glaubst du, daß in diesen noch ein Funke von Vaterlandsliebe lockere? Mit Nichten. Durch den Lurus und die Schwelgerei sind sie so sehr von ihrer Vorfahren Seelengröße herabgewürdigt, daß es ihnen um Freiheit gar nicht mehr zu thun ist. Erst neulich, nach Cäsars Mord, da vorhin Brutus und Cassius auf der Rednerbühne stunden und sie gegen den großen Julius so sehr zum Haß angeflammt hatten, daß sie sich vor Wuth an seinem geheiligten Leichnam fast vergriffen hätten, wie viel Beredsamkeit brauchte ich, ihren Ton anders zu stimmen? Wie Federn lassen sie sich hin und her blasen. Der Soldat ist schon gewöhnt, eben so gut der Bürger als der Feinde Blut zu versprißen, und den haben wir ja auf unserer Seite. Bei dem niedrigen Pöbel ist es mit wenig Worten, etwas Getreide oder Geld und öffentlichen Schauspielen geschehen. Lepidus. Diesen Artikel will ich besorgen. Octavius. Du hast vollkommen Recht, Antonius. Eine Bedenklichkeit ist nun gehoben. Aber ein Brutus, ein Cassius, ist weit über die Sphäre des Pöbels erhaben. Antonius. O die haben durch Cäsar's Mord und meine Rede alles Gewicht, alle Liebe, alles Ansehn verloren. Das Volk ist ja auf unserer Seite. Was können sie also vornehmen? Und bis hieher sind sie ruhig. Octavius. Kaum vor vier Stunden hab ' ich Briefe erhalten, daß sie sich ganz heimlich zu einer Gegenwehr rüsten, weil sie von uns etwas besorgen. Ich wollte dir die Nachricht gleich hinterbringen, aber du warst weder auf dem Capitol noch zu Haus. Antonius. Ich war auf meinem Landgut. Daß aber Brutus und Cassius sich zum Kriege rüsten, macht mir keine so große Besorgniß. Wir sind so gut Krieger als sie. Nur müssen wir auf unserer Hut sein, unsere Kräfte vereinigen und deswegen gleich unsere Legaten und Tribunen zusammen berufen. Octavius. Es giebt aber doch noch außer diesen eine Menge Feinde, die zwar Freundlichkeit im Gesicht blicken lassen, im Herzen hingegen giftige Dolche verbergen. Diese sollten aus dem Weg geräumt sein.
e: Octavius. But I have. I will lay them before you. Will the [p. 452] free Romans consent thus to our rule? Will Brutus, will Cassius, will the others who helped kill the noble Caesar, be quiet about it? Will Sextus Pompeius let himself be satisfied? Antonius. Oh! Octavius, no such scruples! Believe me, I have lived longer in the world, I have more experience than you. Do you believe that in these men a spark of love of fatherland still glows? By no means. Through luxury and debauchery they are so far debased from the greatness of soul of their forefathers that they no longer care at all about freedom. Only recently, after Caesar’s murder, when Brutus and Cassius had just before stood on the speaker’s platform and had so inflamed them to hatred against the great Julius that they would almost have laid hands, in their rage, on his sacred corpse, how much eloquence did I need to tune their tone differently! How like feathers they let themselves be blown to and fro! The soldier is already accustomed to shedding the blood of citizens just as well as of enemies, and him we have indeed on our side. With the low rabble it is done with few words, a little grain or money, and public spectacles. Lepidus. This article I will see to. Octavius. You are perfectly right, Antonius. One scruple is now removed. But a Brutus, a Cassius, is far above the sphere of the rabble. Antonius. Oh, they have lost all weight, all love, all standing through Caesar’s murder and my speech. The people are indeed on our side. What can they therefore undertake? And up to now they are quiet. Octavius. Scarcely four hours ago I received letters that they are arming quite secretly for a defense, because they fear something from us. I meant to bring you the news at once, but you were neither on the Capitol nor at home. Antonius. I was on my country estate. But that Brutus and Cassius are arming for war causes me no such great anxiety. We are as good warriors as they. Only we must be on our guard, unite our forces, and for that reason summon our legates and tribunes together at once. Octavius. But there is yet, besides these, a multitude of enemies who indeed let friendliness show in the face, but in the heart on the contrary conceal poisonous daggers. These should be cleared out of the way.

o: Antonius. Recht, mein Octavius. Wir haben ja auch schon in [p. 453] der lezten Versammlung davon geredet, die meisten genannt und ihnen den Tod geschworen. Hier hab ' ich sie aufgeschrieben. Les't es durch. Octavius (liest es durch und ruft plößlich aus:) Auch Cicero? Antonius. Ja, Octavius. Wir, haben in der lekten Versammlung beschlossen, einem Jeden frei zu lassen, wen er gern in's Todtenreich geschickt hätte. Cicero war mein Todfeind. Seine Reden und Briefe beweisen es nur zu sehr. Und Lepidus hat dir ja sogar seinen Bruder überlassen. Lepidus. Ja, das hab ' ich. Octavius. Mein gegebenes Wort kann ich nimmer zurücknehmen, aber der Mann schmerzt mich außerordentlich. Antonius. Hier, Lepidus, lies auch du es durch. Mein Oheint Lucius steht auf dein Begehren auch unter den Verurtheilten. Es ist also ein Gleichgewicht unter uns. Ieder hat unserem Gemeinwohl einen Mann aufgeopfert, der ihm weh thut. Doch wir wollen uns jezt auf einen andern Gegenstand wenden, nämlich die Theilung der Länder. Octavius. Diesen Punct wollen wir, dünkt mich, für jetzt noch beruhen lassen Erst nach Bezwingung des Brutus und Cassius wollen wir ihn berichtigen.
